objectives: Say what a feeling is in your own words.
Name the feelings you feel most often.
Tell one grown-up how you feel today.
Use the words for feelings when you talk.
Ask for help when a feeling feels too big.
Be kind to a friend who feels sad.

sections.body:
A feeling is a message that comes from inside you. It tells your body and your mind what is going on.

When a feeling comes, you can see it. Your face changes. Your voice changes. Your hands may feel shaky. Your tummy may feel strange. Your body tells the story before your mouth does.

Every child has feelings every day. Some feelings are nice, like happiness. Some feelings are hard, like sadness or fear. Both kinds are normal. A feeling is never bad or naughty. What you do with a feeling is what matters.

Feelings come from two places. Some come from inside you, like hunger and tiredness and excitement. Some come from outside you, like a loud bang, a hot day, or a friend who says no.

You can learn your feelings. First you notice them. Then you give them a name. Then you tell somebody. Then you choose what to do next. That last part is called coping, and it is a skill you can practise.

Naming a feeling makes it smaller. When you say the word for it, it stops being a big fog inside you and becomes a small thing you can look at. That is why grown-ups ask you how you feel. They are not asking to make trouble. They are trying to help.

In this book you will learn the feeling words, you will learn how to tell a grown-up, and you will learn what to do when a feeling feels too big to hold.
examples: I feel a bit sad inside.
My tummy feels funny. I think I am nervous.
sections.heading: What is a feeling?

sections.body:
**Happy** is a warm feeling. It makes you want to smile and share. You feel happy when something good happens, or when somebody is kind to you.

**Sad** is a heavy feeling. It sits in your chest and makes you want to cry. You feel sad when you lose something, or when somebody you love goes far away. Sadness needs time, not fixing.

**Angry** is a hot feeling. It burns in your hands and makes your face tight. You feel angry when somebody takes your thing, says something unkind, or blocks you. Angry is a signal, not a punishment.

**Scared** is a shaky feeling. Your heart beats fast and you want to run or hide. You feel scared in the dark, before a new thing, or when you hear a loud noise.

**Worried** is a thinking feeling. It feels like a question that will not go away. You feel worried about something that has not happened yet, like tomorrow's test.

**Proud** is a warm feeling about yourself. You feel proud when you try hard and get it done. You can feel proud of a good try, even when it goes wrong.

**Shy** is a quiet feeling. You feel shy when you want to join in but are not sure how. Shy is not weak. Shy is just careful.

Some feelings come together. You can feel angry and sad at the same time. That is normal too. You do not have to pick just one.
examples: I feel proud of my drawing.
I feel scared about the school play.
I feel angry and sad at the same time.
sections.heading: The feelings you feel most often

sections.body:
These are the words grown-ups use for feelings. When you know the words, you can say what is inside you.

A **feeling** is what you feel inside your body and mind. A feeling can be nice or hard.

To be **happy** means you feel good inside. You want to smile, sing, or share the good news.

To be **sad** means you feel heavy inside. You might cry, or you might want to be alone for a while.

To be **angry** means you feel hot and upset. Anger shows up fast and it is often about something you need that you did not get.

To be **scared** means you feel afraid of something. Scared tells you to be careful and to look for a grown-up.

To be **worried** means you keep thinking about something that might happen later. Worry is a feeling that will not leave on its own.

To be **upset** means a strong feeling is winning for the moment. It is a good word to use when you cannot decide which feeling it is.

When you cannot find the exact word, say **I feel upset**. That is enough for a grown-up to help you.
examples: I feel a bit shy today.
I feel upset and I do not know why.
sections.heading: The words we use for feelings

terms.gloss: Something that happens inside you. It shows on your face and tells you what you need.

terms.example: I feel happy when my friend sits with me.
terms.gloss: A warm, good feeling inside. It makes you want to smile and share.

terms.example: I feel sad because my cat is away.
terms.gloss: A heavy feeling inside. It often wants tears or quiet time.

terms.example: I feel angry, so I am going to count to ten.
terms.gloss: A hot, upset feeling. It often comes fast and shows in your hands and face.

terms.example: I feel scared in the dark, so I hold my blanket.
terms.gloss: An afraid feeling. Your heart beats fast and you want to run or hide.

sections.body:
Sometimes a feeling arrives and you do not know its name. These four steps help you find it.

First, stop for a moment. Put your hands still. Look at what is around you.

Next, check your body. Is your tummy tight? Is your face hot? Does your heart beat fast? Your body always gives a clue.

Then, ask what just happened. Did somebody help you? Did somebody say no? Did something break? Did you get what you wanted? The answer usually points to the feeling.

Finally, say the word out loud. Pick the closest one. It does not have to be perfect. Being close is good enough to start.

Try this with a small feeling today. Name it once and see how much lighter it feels.
examples: My face feels hot. I am angry.
I feel nervous because of the new school.
I feel tired and grumpy this morning.
sections.heading: How to work out what you feel
steps: Stop for a moment and put your hands still.
Check your body for a clue.
Say the feeling word out loud.

sections.body:
When a friend tells you they feel sad, you do not have to fix it. You can just be there.

Sit next to them. Say you are sorry they feel that way. Offer to listen without fixing anything.

Do not say things like *do not cry* or *cheer up*. Those words tell the person their feeling is wrong. Say instead that you can see they are sad.

Do not laugh at somebody who cries. Do not walk away. Do not tell other people about it.

Sometimes a friend is not ready to talk. Then you can just share a quiet game, sit and draw, or walk together. Presence is a gift.

And if your friend says something is hurting them, or they cannot be safe, you must tell a grown-up. That is not telling a secret. That is being a good friend.
examples: I can see you are sad. Do you want me to sit with you?
You do not have to be okay right now.
I will stay here with you for a bit.
sections.heading: How to be a good friend to someone who feels sad

sections.body:
Some feelings are too big to sit with quietly. Your hands shake. Your face burns. You want to shout, or hit, or run away and hide.

Big feelings come from big moments. Your brother broke your thing. You said no to somebody. A new person walked into your group. The feeling is big because the moment matters to you.

You cannot always make a big feeling smaller right away. You can make your body safe first.

Put your hands on the table. Breathe in slowly through your nose. Count four. Breathe out slowly through your mouth. Count four. Do that three times. Your body cannot shout and breathe slowly at the same time.

Then find words. Say the feeling and ask for help. *I am really angry and I do not know what to do. Can you help me?*

If you might hurt yourself or somebody else, walk away to a safe place and tell a grown-up straight away. You will not get in trouble for asking for help. Grown-ups want to help you.

Feelings do not last forever. The angry feeling fades. The scared feeling shrinks. If you name it, ask for help, and wait, it will pass.
examples: I am really angry. I need a moment.
Can you help me? I do not know what to do.
I need to go and sit by myself for a minute.
sections.heading: What to do when a feeling feels too big

item.summary: A feeling is a message from inside you. After reading this you can name what you feel, say it out loud to a grown-up or a friend, and help a friend who is feeling sad.
